🎭 Calling Card: NASA Space Apps 2026

“The Red Planet holds the treasure. We’re here to take it, and share it with everyone.”

We are Phantom Synkro, a crew of three from SynkroLab, an open-source hardware and scientific democratization lab from Bogotá, Colombia. Our philosophy is simple: knowledge and technology shouldn’t belong to a few. So we build tools, make them open, and put them in everyone’s hands, a bit like Phantom Thieves of science. 🃏

Time to take the heart of Mars. ❤️‍🔥
summary: Martian Map is a browser-based, HUD-style tool that helps a Mars astronaut plan and follow a surface traverse. It blends three kinds of NASA data (optical from Viking, topographic from MOLA, and thermal from THEMIS infrared) with opacity sliders, and adds a Halo-style radar that shows nearby named features by distance and bearing. Users can build routes and get distance, ascent, descent and slope, with elevation estimated anywhere on the map and shown with an error margin. As a ready-made mission, it replays Perseverance's real traverse across Jezero Crater (708 waypoints) and shows NASA raw photos at each stop, so the crew knows what to expect on arrival. For safety, it exposes terrain slope and a relative soil-firmness hint from night infrared data, and it is transparent about the limits of every layer.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Martian Map is an interactive web map designed as a tablet or helmet-visor display for an astronaut exploring Mars on foot. We chose Jezero Crater, an ancient lake and river delta, because Perseverance has driven about 45 km there, which gives us dense real data and photos.

- Layered data: Viking optical mosaic as the base map, with MOLA color topography and THEMIS day/night infrared as overlays. Each overlay has an opacity slider so layers can be combined.

- Halo-style radar: drag the astronaut marker and the radar shows nearby named features (about 2,000, from a Mars nomenclature database) by distance and bearing, with adjustable range. Distances use Mars' radius.

- Route planner: click waypoints to get total distance, ascent, descent and maximum slope.

- Real traverse and photos: 708 Perseverance waypoints (sol 13 to 2022). Clicking one loads raw photos taken at that location from NASA's raw-images API. One button replays the traverse stop by stop, and another copies it into the route planner.

- Terrain hints: with the night-infrared layer on, hovering shows a relative soil-firmness index (rock keeps heat at night, fine dust does not).

HOW IT WORKS

Everything runs in the browser. Map tiles come from NASA Mars Trek (WMTS). Trek does not expose a raw elevation grid, so we estimate elevation from the color of the MOLA color-relief tile. We calibrated the color-to-meters conversion automatically using about 500 named features of known elevation, and validated it with a leave-one-out test: median error of about 100 m, with 97% of points within 1,500 m. The app shows an error margin next to each value, and it grows where color is ambiguous (very high terrain, white pixels). Rover waypoints and elevations come from NASA's published Mars 2020 data.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- Safety first: the crew sees slope, ascent and descent, and a soil-firmness hint before committing to a route, along with honest error margins.

- Preparation: photos from the real traverse show what a stop looks like before arriving.

- Accessibility: no installation or accounts. It runs in any browser using only public NASA data, so students and the public can explore Mars the way a crew would.

TOOLS

JavaScript, HTML and CSS with Leaflet (no build step); NASA Mars Trek tiles (MOLA, Viking, THEMIS); Mars 2020 waypoints and raw-images API; a Python script to build the nomenclature database; VS Code; GitHub and GitHub Pages for hosting.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

- We use a database of named features as ground truth to calibrate and validate elevation from imagery, and we show the error openly.

- A Halo-style radar and HUD layout instead of a conventional GIS viewer.

- A real rover traverse reused as a ready-made mission, with photos at each stop.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED AND LIMITS

We prioritized astronaut safety and honesty about the data. Elevation is estimated, thermal values are relative (infrared brightness, not degrees), and slope is approximate because rover waypoints are close together. Next steps: radiation and weather layers (for example Curiosity RAD and Perseverance MEDA data), a spectral or mineral layer, and automatic obstacle-avoiding routes.
